# Diagnosing Idle Instability in Honda Civic K-Series Engines

When a vehicle transitions from gear to neutral, the engine control unit (ECU) is expected to manage a smooth load change without destabilizing the idle speed controller. In your specific case involving a 2006 Honda Civic DX with a manual transmission, the symptom describes a classic "hunting" behavior where the RPM drops dangerously low (200–400 range) before recovering or stalling entirely. This occurs exclusively when the engine is warm and specifically upon disengaging the clutch, indicating a decoupling issue between the torque converter logic and the idle air control system.

The core of this problem lies in how the ECU calculates target RPM based on coolant temperature (ECT). When cold, the ECU enriches the mixture and raises the base idle to prevent flooding and ensure smooth warm-up; hence your observation of a stable 1000 RPM when the car is cold. Once the engine reaches operating temperature, the ECU targets a lower baseline, typically around 650–750 RPM depending on battery voltage and load conditions. The fact that the idle drops to 200 RPM suggests the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve is either mechanically stuck in its closed position or receiving an erroneous signal telling it to reduce airflow aggressively as part of a stall prevention strategy.

Given your list of modifications—a Cold Air Intake (CAI) and an exhaust system—along with the maintenance you've already performed, we must look at airflow dynamics and sensor data rather than simple fouling. You mentioned changing spark plugs and using injector cleaner; these address combustion quality but do not resolve issues related to air mass measurement or throttle body cleanliness. The CAI is particularly relevant here because it alters the volumetric efficiency of the engine compared to a stock setup, potentially confusing an older ECU if the Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor is dirty or if the intake runner lengths have shifted significantly from factory specifications.

The most probable culprit in this scenario is a throttle body that has accumulated varnish on its bore and the IAC valve pintle. Over time, carbon deposits create a physical restriction. When you shift to neutral, the load drops instantly. The ECU attempts to compensate by opening the IAC valve to admit more air. If the pintle is gummed up with lacquer or if the throttle plate leaves a vacuum leak gap due to warping, the sensor readings might momentarily suggest an over-rich condition or a lean spike, triggering the ECU to cut fuel and close the throttle aggressively, causing the RPM collapse.

Another critical factor involves the Positive Crankcase Ventilation (PCV) system. On many K-series engines from this era, if the PCV valve sticks in the closed position under vacuum load changes, it can create excessive crankcase pressure that robs power from the intake manifold, leading to a sudden stall. Since you have a CAI, ensure the installation did not inadvertently restrict the return path for fresh air or alter the breather dynamics significantly.

To systematically diagnose this, start by inspecting the throttle body bore and IAC valve pintle with a borescope or compressed air before attempting chemical cleaners. A mechanical stickiness in the IAC motor will often prevent it from opening fully to maintain idle. Additionally, verify that all vacuum lines connected to the brake booster and PCV system are free of cracks; a hidden leak only manifests under specific load transitions like shifting to neutral.

If the hardware checks out, the issue may be software-related, specifically an adaptation learning reset. After installing performance parts like a CAI or exhaust, the ECU's long-term fuel trims (LTFT) can drift into incorrect compensation values. Using a diagnostic tool to clear the ECU adaptations and relearn procedures can sometimes resolve these erratic idle behaviors by forcing the system to recalibrate its understanding of airflow versus fuel delivery at higher temperatures.
